key_insight: IELSM replaces trial-and-error lattice elements with a theoretically admissible, polygon-tessellated spring model that achieves isotropic elasticity and fracture simulation through simple node sharing.
engineering_relevance: It offers a practical way to model quasi-brittle cracking in concrete-like materials with better balance of accuracy, efficiency, and mesh compatibility than standard lattice models or full FEM.
method: Discretize the continuum into arbitrary polygonal tessellations with axial springs plus a volumetric constraint to enforce isotropic elasticity.
Derive admissible element shapes from governing equations, enabling regular N-gons and even concave elements.
Couple IELSM with FEM directly by shared nodes, and activate damage only in fracture-prone regions to reduce cost.
evidence_signal: The paper reports pure bending and four fracture benchmarks where IELSM matches experiments and improves crack-path and load–displacement predictions, while hybridizing with FEM cuts nodes by 41.2–80.9% and CPU time by 34.2–85.2%.
watch_item: The approach still depends on a theoretically admissible tessellation and an isotropic damage law, so element selection and parameter calibration may limit robustness for highly heterogeneous or strongly anisotropic materials.
paper_title: Tessellated Isotropic Elastic Lattice Spring Model for Quasi-Brittle Fracture
